title: Who is eldest
hookLine: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant decide by the banyan tree who should be honored (Jataka 37)

cards: A partridge, a monkey and an elephant share a home under a great banyan tree. They're friends, more or less, but they keep stepping on each other: nobody listens, nobody defers, nobody knows whose word should count.
So they agree on a fix. Whoever is oldest gets the honor, and the others will listen to him. Except none of them knows who that is.
The Tittira Jataka is how they find out.

teach.h: THE ELEPHANT: A BUSH I WALKED OVER.
teach.b: First, the elephant. When I was young, he says, this banyan was a little bush. I walked right over it, and its top branches brushed my belly.

teach.h: THE MONKEY: I ATE ITS TOP SHOOTS.
teach.b: Second, the monkey. When I was young, I'd sit on the ground and nibble this banyan's topmost shoots without even stretching my neck. Third, the partridge.
There used to be another great banyan, over in another place.

teach.h: THE PARTRIDGE: I DROPPED THE SEED.
teach.b: I ate one of its fruits, and dropped the seed right here. This tree grew from that. So I knew this tree before it was a tree at all.

The other two agree at once: the partridge is the eldest. From then on they honor him and listen to his advice, and the tale says they lived well together. Each claim is a memory, and the oldest memory wins.
In the present-day story, the Buddha hears that his senior disciple Sariputta spent a night outside, because younger monks had taken every place to sleep.
He tells this tale, and teaches that in the community, places and respect go by seniority in the order, not by birth or status.
Honor here isn't flattery. It's a way of making room, so a crowded home under one tree can get along.

how: In Buddhist monastic communities, monks and nuns are seated and greeted in order of seniority since ordination, and lay Buddhists may greet elders with a bow.

o: rank by who came first, not by status
rank by size, strength or wealth
rank by who gives the best advice

games.q: who is eldest: tap the pairs.
p: walked over the tree when it was a bush
nibbled its top shoots from the ground
dropped the seed it grew from
spent a night outside with no place

s: the elephant was eldest because he was biggest
size didn't decide it; the oldest memory of the tree did, and that was the partridge's.
the partridge said the banyan grew from a seed he dropped
he ate the fruit of another banyan and dropped the seed right there.
the Buddha taught that respect in the order goes by family rank
he taught that it goes by seniority in the order, not by birth or status.

games.q: you're one of three friends under a banyan tree, and you've agreed to honor whoever is oldest. how do you decide?
o: whoever is strongest is clearly in charge.
each says what he remembers of the tree.
games.why: the elephant remembers a bush, the monkey remembers tiny shoots, and the partridge remembers dropping the seed. the partridge is eldest.

practice: Bring to mind someone who was there before you, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, a longtime colleague, someone who remembers the tree as a seed. Hold their face for a few breaths.
Then picture one small way to give them a place, like asking their advice or letting them speak first.

wordCard.voice: Seniority. What a partridge, a monkey and an elephant settle by the oldest memory of their tree, and the partridge wins. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: honor the eldest. The oldest memory belonged to the smallest bird. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 6 (seniority in lodging and salutation)
